details:
**Okonkwo and Chinua Achebe**
Okonkwo is the proud, hot-tempered Igbo protagonist of Things Fall Apart (1958), the debut novel of Nigerian author Chinua Achebe. A self-made man driven by a fear of failure and weakness, he is the most common giveaway for the novel, which traces his rise and downfall in his village of Umuofia.

**Ikemefuna**
A boy from the neighboring village of Mbaino who is given to Umuofia as compensation for the murder of a Umuofia woman and lives in Okonkwo's household for three years, calling him father. When the Oracle decrees his death, Okonkwo strikes the fatal blow with his machete despite the elder Ezeudu's warning not to take part, because he is afraid of looking weak.

**Amalinze the Cat**
A wrestler nicknamed "the Cat" because his back never touched the ground. Okonkwo first gains fame by throwing him in a wrestling match; his second wife, Ekwefi, later leaves her first husband for Okonkwo after watching him wrestle.

**The Week of Peace**
A sacred week before planting in Umuofia during which no harsh word may be spoken. Okonkwo breaks it by beating his youngest wife, Ojiugo, when she neglects to cook his meal, and he is fined by the priest of the earth goddess Ani.

**Okonkwo's exile (Ezeudu's funeral)**
At the funeral of the elder Ezeudu, Okonkwo's gun accidentally explodes and kills Ezeudu's sixteen-year-old son. This "female" (inadvertent) crime forces Okonkwo and his family into a seven-year exile in Mbanta, his mother's village.

**Nwoye / Isaac**
Okonkwo's eldest son, whom he beats and considers lazy and effeminate. Disturbed by Ikemefuna's death, Nwoye is drawn to the Christian missionaries' hymns and converts, taking the name Isaac; he is later sent to a teachers' training college in Umuru.

**Okonkwo's suicide and "The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger"**
After the clan fails to rise against the colonists, Okonkwo kills a court messenger sent to break up a town meeting, realizing that Umuofia "would not go to war," then hangs himself. Because suicide is an abomination, his clansmen cannot touch the body, and Obierika asks the District Commissioner's men to cut it down. The novel ends with the Commissioner deciding Okonkwo merits "perhaps not a whole chapter but a reasonable paragraph" in his planned book, The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger.

**Unoka**
Okonkwo's father, a lazy, debt-ridden flute player who never had enough cowries and was considered an agbala (a man with no title). He died of a swelling in the stomach and was left to die in the Evil Forest. Okonkwo's whole life is a reaction against his father's weakness.

**Ezinma, Ekwefi, and Chielo**
Ezinma is the only surviving child of Ekwefi, who had lost nine (Ezinma is the tenth) children in infancy, a misfortune blamed on an ogbanje, a spirit child who keeps dying and being reborn; Ezinma's buried iyi-uwa (spirit stone) is dug up to break the cycle. Chielo, priestess of Agbala, the Oracle of the Hills and the Caves, carries Ezinma on her back through nine villages to the oracle's cave at night, while Ekwefi follows. Okonkwo wishes Ezinma had been born a boy.

**Mr. Brown and Reverend James Smith**
Two Christian missionaries. The tolerant Mr. Brown builds a school and a hospital and has friendly debates about religion with the clansman Akunna. His successor, the strict Reverend James Smith, is uncompromising, and his zealous convert Enoch provokes the clan's anger.

**Enoch unmasks an egwugwu**
The fanatical convert Enoch tears the mask off an egwugwu, a masked ancestral spirit, which is a grave sacrilege. In response the egwugwu burn down Mr. Smith's church, and the District Commissioner later jails Okonkwo and other leaders, holding them for a ransom of two hundred bags of cowries.

**Ekwefi and the banana leaves**
Ekwefi, Okonkwo's second wife, cuts leaves from a banana tree to wrap food before a festival. Okonkwo beats her, and when she mutters about "guns that never shot," he fires his gun at her and misses.

**The tortoise and the birds**
Ekwefi tells Ezinma the folktale of Tortoise, who borrows feathers to attend a feast in the sky, renames himself "All of you," and eats the food meant for the birds. The angry birds take back their feathers, and Tortoise falls onto the hard objects in his compound, explaining why his shell is not smooth. Okonkwo also remembers his mother's tale of Mosquito and Ear.

**The "iron horse" and Abame**
The people of Abame kill the first white man they see, riding a bicycle they call an "iron horse," and tie it to their sacred tree. In retaliation, white soldiers massacre the village during market day, a story Obierika brings to Okonkwo during his exile.

**No Longer at Ease and the title's source**
The novel's title comes from W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming." Its sequel, No Longer at Ease, takes its title from T. S. Eliot's "Journey of the Magi" and follows Okonkwo's grandson Obi, an English-educated civil servant who loves the osu (outcast) Clara and takes bribes. Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's short story "The Headstrong Historian" responds to Things Fall Apart by centering the women who stay in its background.
